Decide whether to suction the client's airway
rationales: Incorrect. Assessing swallowing is an assessment that the nurse must perform.
Incorrect. Evaluating a change in neurologic status requires nursing judgment.
Correct. Repositioning every 2 hours is routine care listed in the book that an AP can carry out.
Incorrect. Deciding when to suction requires nursing assessment of the airway.
questions.clue: Only one task is routine and requires no assessment or judgment.
questions.priority: Delegate routine care; keep assessment and evaluation with the nurse.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client recovering from a stroke says, "He cries and gets upset over small things now. He was never like this before." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "He is probably doing this to get extra attention."
"This means another stroke is starting, so I will call a rapid response."
"Try to ignore it, and it will stop on its own."
"Emotional changes can happen after a stroke. Let's talk about how this is affecting you both."
rationales: Incorrect. This dismisses a recognized effect of the stroke and blames the client.
Incorrect. Emotional changes alone are a known complication, not a sign of a new stroke.
Incorrect. Telling the spouse to ignore the behavior gives no support or understanding.
Correct. The book lists emotional changes among stroke complications; explaining this and inviting discussion supports the family.
questions.clue: The client's emotional changes began after the stroke.
questions.priority: Support the family by explaining expected emotional changes after stroke.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client's family about the warning signs of stroke. Which statement by a family member shows correct understanding?
options: "If his arm feels weak, I will let him rest and check again tomorrow."
"If his face droops and his speech slurs, I will call 911 right away."
"If he has trouble speaking, I will drive him to his clinic next week."
"If his symptoms go away in a few minutes, there is no need to tell anyone."
rationales: Incorrect. Waiting delays treatment; irreversible brain injury can occur within minutes.
Correct. The book stresses calling 911 immediately because time lost is brain lost.
Incorrect. A delayed clinic visit wastes the treatment window.
Incorrect. Symptoms that resolve can still be a TIA and need to be reported.
questions.clue: Stroke signs require immediate emergency activation.
questions.priority: Teach families to call 911 immediately because time lost is brain lost.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Which task can the nurse assign to an assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Check the pupils for size and reaction
Keep the client's head midline and neutral when repositioning
Interpret the reading on the ICP monitor
Give the prescribed mannitol dose
rationales: Incorrect. Pupil checks are a neurologic assessment the nurse must perform.
Correct. Keeping the head midline and neutral is a listed intervention that an AP can carry out when helping with care.
Incorrect. Interpreting ICP readings requires nursing judgment.
Incorrect. Giving medications is not within the AP role.
questions.clue: Only one task is routine positioning without assessment.
questions.priority: Delegate routine positioning; keep assessment and medications with the nurse.

questions.stem: A client with a traumatic brain injury has an ICP monitoring device. The current reading is 24 mm Hg. How should the nurse interpret this reading?
options: It is within the normal range
It is above the normal range
It is below the normal range
It cannot be interpreted without a CT scan
rationales: Incorrect. The book gives normal ICP as 5-15 mm Hg, so 24 is not normal.
Correct. Normal ICP is 5-15 mm Hg, so 24 mm Hg is elevated.
Incorrect. A reading of 24 mm Hg is higher, not lower, than 5-15 mm Hg.
Incorrect. The reading can be compared directly with the normal range.
questions.clue: The ICP reading is 24 mm Hg.
questions.priority: Compare ICP readings with the normal range of 5-15 mm Hg.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a group of newly admitted clients. Which clients have a condition that can cause increased intracranial pressure? Select all that apply.
options: A client with hydrocephalus
A client with seasonal allergies
A client with bacterial meningitis
A client with a brain tumor
A client admitted after a stroke
A client with a sprained wrist
rationales: Correct. Hydrocephalus is listed as a cause of increased ICP.
Incorrect. Seasonal allergies are not a cause of increased ICP.
Correct. Infections such as meningitis are listed causes of increased ICP.
Correct. Brain tumors are listed as a cause of increased ICP.
Correct. Stroke is listed as a cause of increased ICP.
Incorrect. A wrist sprain does not affect pressure inside the skull.
questions.clue: Several clients have conditions inside the skull.
questions.priority: Recognize clients at risk for increased ICP so they are monitored closely.

questions.stem: A client with increased intracranial pressure received interventions 2 hours ago. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or worsening.
rows: Client is now awake and answers questions
Pupils are equal and react briskly
Pulse pressure is widening
Heart rate has dropped to 46/min
ICP monitor reads 12 mm Hg
rationales: Improvement. A falling level of consciousness is the first sign of worsening, so a more alert client is improving.
Improvement. Sluggish, unequal pupils are a sign of rising ICP; equal, brisk pupils show improvement.
Worsening. A widened pulse pressure is part of Cushing's triad, a late sign.
Worsening. Bradycardia is part of Cushing's triad.
Improvement. 12 mm Hg is within the normal range of 5-15 mm Hg.
questions.clue: Compare each finding with the early and late signs of increased ICP.
questions.priority: Evaluate response to ICP treatment by LOC, pupils, vital signs and ICP reading.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing an SBAR report about a client with a head injury. Which assessment finding is most important to include in the report?
options: The client was alert 1 hour ago and now opens the eyes only to voice
The client has had a mild headache since admission
The client ate half of the breakfast tray
The client asked for an extra blanket
rationales: Correct. A sudden drop in LOC is the first critical sign of worsening ICP and must be reported.
Incorrect. Headache was present on admission and is not a new change.
Incorrect. Intake is useful but not urgent.
Incorrect. Comfort requests are not a critical change.
questions.clue: The client's level of consciousness has suddenly decreased.
questions.priority: Report a sudden drop in LOC promptly; it is the first sign of worsening ICP.

questions.stem: A client with increased intracranial pressure has not had a bowel movement in 3 days and is bearing down hard on the bedpan. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the client to stop bearing down because straining can raise ICP
Encourage the client to push harder to finish quickly
Lower the head of the bed flat to help with elimination
Have the client pull the knees tightly to the chest
rationales: Correct. The book says to avoid straining because it increases ICP.
Incorrect. Pushing harder increases straining, which raises ICP.
Incorrect. The head of the bed should stay at 30 degrees, not flat.
Incorrect. Sharp hip flexion should be avoided because it raises ICP.
questions.clue: The client is straining during elimination.
questions.priority: Prevent increases in ICP by avoiding straining and hip flexion.

questions.stem: A client with increased intracranial pressure received mannitol. Which finding best shows that the drug is having the desired effect?
options: Pulse pressure widens
Pupils become fixed and dilated
Heart rate falls from 80 to 50/min
ICP reading falls from 22 to 13 mm Hg
rationales: Incorrect. A widening pulse pressure is part of Cushing's triad.
Incorrect. Fixed, dilated pupils are a late sign of rising ICP.
Incorrect. Bradycardia is part of Cushing's triad and shows worsening.
Correct. Mannitol is given to lower ICP, and 13 mm Hg is within the normal range of 5-15 mm Hg.
questions.clue: The desired effect of an osmotic diuretic in this client is a lower ICP.
questions.priority: Evaluate mannitol by a return of ICP toward 5-15 mm Hg.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with seizure disorders. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client who has had repeated seizures for 10 minutes without waking between them
A client with epilepsy who asks for help filling out a seizure diary
A client who had one seizure this morning and is now awake and talking
A client who reports feeling tired after a seizure 3 hours ago
rationales: Correct. Repeated seizures without recovery describe status epilepticus, which the book calls a life-threatening emergency.
Incorrect. Teaching can wait until emergencies are handled.
Incorrect. This client has recovered and is stable.
Incorrect. Postictal fatigue hours later is expected and not urgent.
questions.clue: One client is having repeated seizures without recovery between them.
questions.priority: Status epilepticus is a life-threatening emergency and takes priority.

questions.stem: A client has just finished a generalized seizure and the airway is clear. Which assessments should the nurse perform now? Select all that apply.
options: Check pupil size and gaze direction
Inspect the tongue and mouth for injury
Give the client water to check swallowing right away
Hold the limbs firmly to test strength
Note the seizure type and how long it lasted
Assess mental status and muscle tone
rationales: Correct. The book lists pupil size and gaze direction in the physical examination during and after a seizure.
Correct. Tongue and mouth injury are listed assessments after a seizure.
Incorrect. Fluids are not part of the listed assessment, and a drowsy client may not swallow safely.
Incorrect. The book says not to restrain the client; holding limbs is not a strength assessment.
Correct. The book says to document seizure type and duration.
Correct. Mental status and muscle tone are part of the post-seizure examination.
questions.clue: The seizure has ended, and the airway is secure.
questions.priority: After a seizure, assess neurologic status and injury, and document the event.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking a history from a client with newly diagnosed epilepsy. Which question best helps the nurse identify the client's seizure triggers?
options: "Have you ever had your cholesterol checked?"
"What is your favorite type of exercise?"
"What do you usually eat for breakfast?"
"Do flashing lights or being very tired seem to come before your seizures?"
rationales: Incorrect. Cholesterol is not a listed seizure trigger.
Incorrect. This does not ask about seizure triggers.
Incorrect. Breakfast foods are not a seizure trigger the book asks about.
Correct. The book lists lights, fatigue and dizziness as triggers or auras to ask about.
questions.clue: The nurse wants to identify triggers that come before seizures.
questions.priority: Identify seizure triggers so the client can avoid them.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a client's home medication list. Which drugs should the nurse recognize as anticonvulsants? Select all that apply.
options: Gabapentin
Valproate
Lamotrigine
Carbamazepine
Warfarin
Clopidogrel
rationales: Correct. Gabapentin is listed as an anticonvulsant.
Correct. Valproate is listed as an anticonvulsant.
Correct. Lamotrigine is listed as an anticonvulsant.
Correct. Carbamazepine is listed as an anticonvulsant.
Incorrect. Warfarin is an anticoagulant.
Incorrect. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet used for clot prevention.
questions.clue: The list mixes anticonvulsants with clot-prevention drugs.
questions.priority: Recognize anticonvulsants on a medication list.

questions.stem: A client's status epilepticus has stopped after IV lorazepam. Which medication should the nurse anticipate next to maintain seizure control?
options: Fosphenytoin
Alteplase
Mannitol
Atropine
rationales: Correct. The book lists phenytoin or fosphenytoin for maintenance after the seizure is stopped.
Incorrect. Alteplase is a clot-busting drug used in ischemic stroke.
Incorrect. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used for increased ICP.
Incorrect. Atropine is not used for seizure maintenance.
questions.clue: The seizure has stopped, and maintenance therapy is now needed.
questions.priority: After stopping status epilepticus, start maintenance anticonvulsant therapy.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews possible causes of seizures in several clients. For each condition, indicate the category of cause the book places it in.
rows: Cerebral aneurysm
Hypertensive encephalopathy
Benzodiazepine withdrawal
SCN1A gene mutation
Fragile X syndrome
rationales: Primary CNS disorder. Aneurysms are listed with tumors, abscesses and AV malformations.
Metabolic/systemic. Hypertensive encephalopathy is listed with febrile states and hyperthermia.
Metabolic/systemic. Drug overdose or withdrawal, including benzodiazepines, is a metabolic/systemic cause.
Genetic. The book names SCN1A, a sodium channel mutation, as a common genetic cause.
Genetic. Fragile X syndrome is listed as a linked genetic condition.
questions.clue: Each cause fits one of the book's cause categories.
questions.priority: Classify seizure causes to guide the search for a treatable cause.

questions.stem: The charge nurse observes a newly hired nurse caring for a client during and after a seizure. For each action, indicate whether it is appropriate or needs follow-up.
rows: Documents the seizure type and how long it lasted
Checks pupil size and gaze direction after the seizure
Forces an oral airway between the clenched teeth during the seizure
Asks the roommate who saw the seizure start to describe it
Removes the suction equipment from the bedside once the seizure ends
rationales: Appropriate. The book says to document seizure type and duration.
Appropriate. Pupil size and gaze direction are listed post-seizure assessments.
Needs follow-up. The book says not to put anything in the mouth during a seizure.
Appropriate. The book says to interview the client and witnesses.
Needs follow-up. Suction should stay at the bedside as part of seizure precautions.
questions.clue: The new nurse's actions are a mix of correct and unsafe practices.
questions.priority: Supervise staff and correct unsafe seizure care.

questions.stem: The parent of a teenager with epilepsy says, "Since the diagnosis, she stays in her room and won't see her friends." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Acknowledge that epilepsy can affect emotions and social life, and offer emotional support for the teen and family
Tell the parent that this is just normal teenage behavior
Advise the parent to keep the teen home from school to avoid seizures in public
Tell the parent that the teen will outgrow these feelings once the seizures stop
rationales: Correct. The book notes epilepsy has psychological and social impacts and lists emotional support as a nursing action.
Incorrect. This dismisses a social change that the book links to epilepsy.
Incorrect. Isolating the teen adds to the social impact rather than supporting coping.
Incorrect. This gives false reassurance and does not address current feelings.
questions.clue: The teen is withdrawing socially after the epilepsy diagnosis.
questions.priority: Address the psychological and social impact of epilepsy with emotional support.

questions.stem: A client with a history of tonic-clonic seizures is admitted for medication adjustment. Which measure should the nurse put in place on admission?
options: Apply wrist restraints at night
Tape a padded tongue blade to the headboard for use during a seizure
Pad the side rails and keep suction equipment at the bedside
Keep the client on strict bed rest with the lights off
rationales: Incorrect. The book says not to restrain a client during a seizure.
Incorrect. The book says not to put anything in the mouth.
Correct. Padded side rails and suction at the bedside are listed nursing measures.
Incorrect. Strict bed rest in the dark is not a listed seizure precaution.
questions.clue: The client is at risk for a seizure during the hospital stay.
questions.priority: Put seizure precautions in place before a seizure happens.

questions.stem: An adult client is admitted after a first seizure with no known cause. Which laboratory tests should the nurse anticipate to help identify a cause?
options: Thyroid antibodies and vitamin D level
Lipid panel and hemoglobin A1C only
Glucose, calcium, BUN, electrolytes and a toxic screen
Troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide
rationales: Incorrect. These are not among the listed seizure work-up tests.
Incorrect. These are not the listed tests for finding a seizure cause.
Correct. The book lists glucose, calcium, BUN, electrolytes and metabolic/toxic screens to identify seizure causes.
Incorrect. These are cardiac markers, not the listed seizure work-up.
questions.clue: The cause of this first seizure is unknown.
questions.priority: Look for metabolic and toxic causes of a new seizure.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client admitted with suspected acute meningitis. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.
options: Nuchal rigidity
Fever with severe headache
Pain in the back of the thigh when the knee is extended with the hip flexed
Clear cerebrospinal fluid with normal glucose and protein
Photophobia
rationales: Correct. Nuchal rigidity is a classic sign of meningitis.
Correct. Headache and fever are classic signs of meningitis.
Correct. This describes a positive Kernig sign.
Incorrect. Clear CSF with normal glucose and protein is the normal finding on p.136; meningitis causes cloudy CSF, low glucose and high protein.
Correct. Photophobia is listed among acute meningitis symptoms.
questions.clue: The client has signs of meningeal irritation.
questions.priority: Recognize classic signs and a positive Kernig test in meningitis.

questions.stem: A client with suspected bacterial meningitis has a patent airway and stable breathing. The nurse has four new prescriptions. Which should the nurse carry out first?
options: Teach the family about vaccinations
Give the first dose of IV ceftriaxone
Draw blood for liver function tests
Schedule a chest x-ray
rationales: Incorrect. Education is important but can wait until treatment has started.
Correct. The book calls rapid antibiotics plus airway protection the top priorities in bacterial meningitis.
Incorrect. Liver function tests are supporting labs; they do not come before the first antibiotic dose.
Incorrect. A chest x-ray is a supporting test, not the first action.
questions.clue: The airway is secure, and the client has suspected bacterial meningitis.
questions.priority: After airway protection, rapid IV antibiotics are the top priority.

questions.stem: A child is admitted with Haemophilus influenzae meningitis. The parent says the child's younger sibling has not received any vaccines. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
options: "Vaccines are only needed after a child turns 5."
"Meningitis cannot spread between children in the same home."
"Bring the sibling's vaccinations up to date, because vaccines have reduced meningitis rates."
"The sibling only needs a vaccine if a fever develops."
rationales: Incorrect. The book does not support delaying vaccination.
Incorrect. Bacterial meningitis requires droplet precautions because it can spread.
Correct. The book lists unvaccinated children as at risk for Haemophilus influenzae and stresses the importance of vaccination.
Incorrect. Vaccines are given to prevent infection, not after symptoms appear.
questions.clue: The sibling is unvaccinated, and the book links unvaccinated children to Haemophilus influenzae meningitis.
questions.priority: Health promotion: vaccination lowers meningitis risk.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews lumbar puncture results for a client with suspected meningitis. For each CSF finding, indicate whether it is consistent with meningitis or within normal limits.
rows: Cloudy, hazy fluid
WBC count of 350/mcL
Glucose of 28 mg/dL
Protein of 30 mg/dL
Positive Gram stain
rationales: Consistent with meningitis. Cloudy or hazy CSF is a listed meningitis finding.
Consistent with meningitis. The book lists elevated WBCs above 200/mcL.
Consistent with meningitis. The book lists low glucose below 45 mg/dL.
Within normal limits. Protein of 30 mg/dL falls in the normal range of 15-50 mg/dL.
Consistent with meningitis. A positive Gram stain identifies the organism type.
questions.clue: Compare each CSF value with the normal values and meningitis findings.
questions.priority: Interpret CSF results to support the diagnosis of meningitis.

questions.stem: A client with bacterial meningitis has a temperature of 39.6 C (103.3 F). Which approach to fever care should the nurse use?
options: Place the client in an ice bath to drop the temperature quickly
Withhold all fever care until culture results are known
Lower the temperature gradually with the prescribed measures
Add extra blankets to stop the client from shivering
rationales: Incorrect. The book says to treat fever gradually, not rapidly.
Incorrect. Fever care should not wait for cultures.
Correct. The book lists treating fever gradually as part of meningitis care.
Incorrect. Extra blankets would hold in heat and raise the temperature.
questions.clue: The client has a high fever from bacterial meningitis.
questions.priority: Reduce fever gradually in meningitis.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client with bacterial meningitis stands at the doorway looking frightened and asks, "Is there anything I can do to help?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "It is best if you wait in the lobby until the client is better."
"Please do not ask questions, since the client needs complete silence."
"There is nothing you can do right now, so try not to worry."
"You can sit with your spouse and talk quietly while I explain what we are doing."
rationales: Incorrect. Sending the spouse away ignores the book's call for family involvement.
Incorrect. This blocks communication instead of offering support.
Incorrect. This dismisses the spouse's fear and excludes the family.
Correct. The book lists emotional support and family involvement in meningitis nursing care; a quiet room is kept for seizure precautions.
questions.clue: The spouse is frightened and wants to help.
questions.priority: Support the family emotionally and involve them in care.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing exposure histories for several clients with suspected viral encephalitis. For each history, indicate the arbovirus the book associates with it.
rows: A child from a rural area in the Midwest
A client recently bitten by a tick
A client from New England with the deadliest form of arbovirus encephalitis
A child with mosquito bites after a summer in the rural Midwest
rationales: La Crosse virus. The book describes it as common in the Midwest in children in rural areas.
Powassan virus. The book lists Powassan as tick-borne.
Eastern equine encephalitis. The book calls EEE the deadliest form and places it in New England.
La Crosse virus. Rural Midwestern children are the group the book links to La Crosse virus.
questions.clue: Age, region and type of insect exposure point to the likely virus.
questions.priority: Use exposure history to identify encephalitis risk.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with HSV encephalitis, fever and signs of rising intracranial pressure. Which medications should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.

Pyridostigmine
A diuretic
Acyclovir
Alteplase

Incorrect. Alteplase is a clot-busting drug for ischemic stroke, not encephalitis.
questions.clue: The client needs antiviral therapy plus supportive care for fever and ICP.
questions.priority: Anticipate antivirals and supportive medications in encephalitis.

questions.stem: A client with encephalitis becomes less responsive and now has snoring respirations. Which action should the nurse take first?

Give the next dose of acyclovir early
Open and maintain the airway
Prepare the client for an MRI
rationales: Incorrect. Lab work does not address the immediate airway problem.

questions.stem: A client recovering from encephalitis is confused and spends most of the day in bed. Which intervention best prevents a complication the book lists for encephalitis?

Keep the client in one comfortable position
Turn and reposition the client on a regular schedule
Keep the head of the bed flat at all times

Incorrect. A flat bed does not prevent pressure ulcers and is not recommended for clients at risk for increased ICP.

questions.priority: Prevent immobility-related complications such as pressure ulcers.

questions.stem: The adult child of a client recovering from encephalitis says, "Mom acts so differently now. I don't know what's happening to her." Which response by the nurse is most helpful?

"You should visit less often so she can rest."
"This has nothing to do with her illness."

Incorrect. This offers false reassurance.
Incorrect. Reducing visits does not support the family or the client.

questions.clue: The family member is distressed by the client's behavior changes.
questions.priority: Help families understand behavioral changes after encephalitis.

questions.stem: A client with suspected encephalitis has had two seizures. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate to evaluate the client's electrical brain activity?

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of CSF
Complete blood count (CBC)
Electroencephalogram (EEG)

questions.stem: A client with a spinal cord injury has paralysis of the legs and bladder and bowel dysfunction. For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Intermittent catheterization
A bowel program with stool softeners and suppositories
Range-of-motion exercises
Splints for the extremities
Keeping the legs still to avoid stretching the muscles
rationales: Indicated. The book lists intermittent catheterization for bladder management.

questions.priority: Prevent contractures and manage elimination after spinal cord injury.

Wait to catheterize until the client says the bladder feels full
Follow a bowel program to prevent impaction
Inspect the skin regularly for injury
Leave the client in one position for long periods to reduce stimulation

questions.clue: Autonomic dysreflexia is triggered by a full bladder, bowel impaction or skin injury.
questions.priority: Prevent autonomic dysreflexia by removing its common triggers.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a spinal cord injury who needs a scheduled bowel program
A client with a traumatic brain injury who is now vomiting and harder to wake
A client with a spinal cord injury who needs range-of-motion exercises

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several clients with Alzheimer disease. For each finding, indicate the stage it best matches.

New anxiety and emotional changes
Aphasia, apraxia and incontinence
Loss of impulse control with vulgar language
Immobility in a fetal position with contractures

questions.stem: A client was diagnosed with early Alzheimer disease 6 months ago. The nurse wants to evaluate whether the client's cognition has changed since diagnosis. Which tool is most appropriate?

Folstein Mini-Mental State Exam
Glasgow Coma Scale only
Brain biopsy

questions.stem: The nurse on a memory care unit receives report on four clients with Alzheimer disease. Which client should the nurse see first?

A client with mild disease who misplaced reading glasses
A client with moderate disease who is incontinent of urine
A client with mild disease who is anxious about a family visit

questions.priority: Assess first the client with a potentially unstable airway after a seizure.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with moderate Alzheimer disease. Which task can the nurse assign to an assistive personnel (AP)?

Remind the client of the day and time using the wall calendar and clock
Assess a new change in the client's level of confusion
Teach the spouse about a durable power of attorney

questions.clue: Only one task is routine and requires no assessment, evaluation or teaching.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing medications for clients with Alzheimer disease. For each medication, indicate the main target of therapy.

questions.clue: Each drug class in the book has a different therapeutic target.
questions.priority: Know the purpose of each medication used in Alzheimer disease.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the spouse of a client who was prescribed donepezil. Which statement by the spouse shows correct understanding?

questions.priority: Evaluate teaching about the purpose of cholinesterase inhibitors.

questions.stem: A client with severe (stage 4) Alzheimer disease is admitted to a long-term care facility. Based on the features of this stage, which safety measure should the nurse include in the plan of care?

Unsupervised walks outside
A bedside razor for self-shaving
Seizure precautions
rationales: Incorrect. Removing side rails does not address the seizure risk; padded rails are part of seizure precautions.

questions.priority: Anticipate stage-specific complications and put precautions in place.

questions.stem: A client with moderate Alzheimer disease is admitted to the hospital and is restless at night. Which actions should the nurse take to keep the client safe? Select all that apply.

Use night lights and security items for night wandering

Leave the client alone in the shower to promote independence

Incorrect. The book calls for a consistent environment; frequent moves increase confusion.

Incorrect. The client needs supervision during ADLs for safety.
questions.clue: The client has moderate disease and is restless at night in an unfamiliar place.
questions.priority: Keep the environment consistent and supervised to prevent injury.

questions.stem: A client with moderate Alzheimer disease becomes upset when the assistive personnel tries to give a bath. Which approach should the nurse recommend?

Use simple, one-step requests and stay calm
Firmly insist that the bath must happen now
Explain in detail why hygiene matters to health

questions.clue: The client becomes upset during an ADL.
questions.priority: Use simple requests and a calm approach during personal care.

questions.stem: A client recently diagnosed with early Alzheimer disease says, "I'm scared of losing myself. I don't know how to face this." Which response by the nurse is best?

"Don't think about that now. Focus on today."
"Your family will handle all of the decisions from now on."
"Many people never get worse, so try not to worry."

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with Parkinson disease. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or unexpected for this condition.

Monotone speech
Tremor that occurs only during purposeful movement

questions.stem: A client being evaluated for Parkinson disease says, "My MRI came back normal, so I must not have Parkinson's." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

"The MRI must be repeated until it shows changes."
"Only a brain biopsy can confirm Parkinson disease in a living person."

Incorrect. The book says MRI/CT are typically normal in PD and are not used for diagnosis.
Incorrect. Repeating the MRI is not how PD is diagnosed.
Incorrect. The book does not describe biopsy for PD diagnosis.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients with Parkinson disease. Which client should the nurse assess first?

questions.priority: Prevent aspiration in PD with swallowing therapy and soft, frequent meals.

questions.stem: A client with Parkinson disease says the tremor started in the right hand 2 years ago and now affects both hands. How should the nurse interpret this history?

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a client with Parkinson disease. For each task, indicate whether it can be assigned to the assistive personnel (AP) or should be done by the nurse.

Evaluate the client's response to carbidopa-levodopa

Assign to AP. Offering prescribed supplemental shakes is routine nutritional care.
Nurse. Assessing swallowing after choking requires nursing assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing medications for clients with multiple sclerosis. For each medication, indicate its main purpose.

A neurologist for a new MRI

"Emotional lability, or sudden mood changes, is a common finding in MS. Let's talk about how it is affecting your family."
rationales: Incorrect. This mislabels a common MS finding.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the medication list of a client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Which medications are used in ALS care? Select all that apply.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Which findings place the client at risk for aspiration? Select all that apply.
options: Finger cramping
Drooling
Dysphagia

Choking during meals
rationales: Incorrect. Finger cramping is an upper-extremity symptom, not a swallowing problem.
Correct. Drooling is a bulbar symptom that signals poor control of secretions.
Correct. Dysphagia is a listed bulbar symptom.
Correct. Slurred speech and tongue involvement reflect bulbar weakness that also affects swallowing.
Correct. Choking is a listed bulbar symptom.
questions.clue: Bulbar symptoms affect speech and swallowing.
questions.priority: Recognize bulbar findings that raise aspiration risk in ALS.

questions.stem: A client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has several new findings. For each finding, indicate the safety risk it most directly creates.
rows: Tripping and stumbling when walking
Choking during meals
An abnormal breathing pattern with diminished breath sounds
An awkward gait
rationales: Falls. Tripping and stumbling are lower-extremity signs that raise fall risk.
Aspiration. Choking is a bulbar symptom that leads to aspiration.
Respiratory failure. The book says to check rate, pattern and breath sounds to monitor for failure.
Falls. An awkward gait is a lower-extremity sign that raises fall risk.
questions.clue: Each finding threatens safety in a different way.
questions.priority: Link ALS findings to the safety risk they create.

questions.stem: A client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) who often tripped at home was given a walker and a set daily routine. Which finding best shows the plan is working?
options: The client's fasciculations have stopped
The client has had no falls in the past month
The client's speech has become clearer
The client has regained strength in both feet
rationales: Incorrect. A walker does not affect fasciculations.
Correct. Mobility aids and routines are meant to keep the client safe, so no falls shows the goal is met.
Incorrect. Speech is not the target of this plan.
Incorrect. ALS is progressive; mobility aids do not restore strength.
questions.clue: The plan targeted tripping and falls.
questions.priority: Evaluate fall-prevention measures by the absence of falls.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Which task can the nurse assign to the assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Check breath sounds and respiratory pattern
Teach the client breathing techniques
Help the client follow the established morning routine
Score the client on the ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised
rationales: Incorrect. A respiratory assessment is a nursing responsibility.
Incorrect. Teaching is a nursing responsibility.
Correct. Helping with an established daily routine is routine care an AP can provide.
Incorrect. The functional rating scale is an assessment that the nurse completes.
questions.clue: Only one task follows an established plan without assessment or teaching.
questions.priority: Delegate routine ADL support; keep assessment and teaching with the nurse.

questions.stem: The nurse is coordinating care for a client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). For each need, indicate the part of the collaborative plan that best addresses it.
rows: The client wants to keep doing as much as possible for as long as possible
The client and family want help planning for the client's end-of-life wishes
The client has increasing respiratory difficulty
The client has new trouble climbing stairs and wants to stay active
rationales: Rehabilitation. The book says rehabilitation focuses on exercise to maintain function.
Palliative care. The book says to collaborate with palliative care on patient and family wishes.
Airway management with NIV. The book lists noninvasive ventilation, possibly followed by mechanical ventilation.
Rehabilitation. The book says rehabilitation focuses on exercise to maintain function.
questions.clue: Each need matches a different part of the ALS collaborative plan.
questions.priority: Coordinate the right team resource for each ALS care need.

questions.stem: A client with advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can communicate with a letter board. The family asks the nurse to let them decide about mechanical ventilation without involving the client. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Agree, because the client can no longer speak
Explain that loss of speech does not mean loss of decision-making, and include the client in the decision
Ask the provider to decide for the family
Delay the discussion until the client can no longer communicate
rationales: Incorrect. Loss of speech does not mean the client cannot decide; this client communicates with a letter board.
Correct. ALS mainly destroys motor neurons (p.146), and this client can still communicate; the nurse advocates for the client's right to take part in care decisions.
Incorrect. The decision belongs to the client, not the provider or family.
Incorrect. Waiting removes the client's chance to direct care.
questions.clue: The client can still communicate with a letter board.
questions.priority: Advocate for the client's right to make care decisions.

questions.stem: A client with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has finger weakness and cramping and has trouble buttoning a shirt. Which action by the nurse best supports self-care?
options: Teach self-care techniques and provide aids for daily activities
Dress the client every morning to save time
Tell the client to wear the same shirt for several days
Restrict use of the hands to prevent cramping
rationales: Correct. The book lists teaching self-care techniques and providing aids and routines for ADLs.
Incorrect. Doing all care takes away the client's independence.
Incorrect. This neglects hygiene and does not solve the problem.
Incorrect. The book focuses on exercise to maintain function.
questions.clue: The client has upper-extremity weakness that limits dressing.
questions.priority: Support independence in ADLs with techniques and aids.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the rehabilitation plan with a client who has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Which client statement shows correct understanding?
options: "I should stop all exercise because it will speed up the disease."
"Exercise will cure the muscle weakness."
"My exercise program is meant to help me keep the function I have."
"I only need to exercise if I lose sensation."
rationales: Incorrect. The book promotes exercise in rehabilitation.
Incorrect. ALS is progressive, and exercise does not cure it.
Correct. The book says rehabilitation focuses on exercise to maintain function.
Incorrect. ALS does not cause sensory loss.
questions.clue: The client is describing the purpose of rehabilitation.
questions.priority: Evaluate understanding of exercise to maintain function in ALS.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) asks, "Will I lose my mind as my body gets weaker?" Which response by the nurse is accurate and supportive?
options: "Yes, memory loss usually comes first."
"ALS mainly affects muscle control, and most people keep clear thinking. What worries you most?"
"Let's not talk about that today."
"It is too early to know anything about ALS."
rationales: Incorrect. Memory loss is not the usual first sign; ALS begins with painless muscle weakness.
Correct. ALS mainly causes loss of motor neurons (p.146); most clients keep clear thinking, although some develop changes in thinking or behavior. Inviting the client to share worries offers support.
Incorrect. This avoids the client's concern.
Incorrect. The book gives clear information about which functions ALS affects.
questions.clue: The client fears losing cognitive function.
questions.priority: Give accurate information and invite the client to express fears.

questions.stem: A client with ascending weakness that began 2 weeks ago has a lumbar puncture. The CSF protein is 380 mg/dL, and lymphocytes are 10/mcL. How should the nurse interpret these results?
options: They are within normal limits
They suggest bacterial meningitis because the white cell count is high
They rule out Guillain-Barre syndrome because protein rises only after 6 months
They are consistent with Guillain-Barre syndrome: high protein with little or no rise in white cells
rationales: Incorrect. Normal CSF protein is 15-60 mg/dL, so 380 mg/dL is high.
Incorrect. Lymphocytes of 10/mcL are a minimal rise, not a high white cell count.
Incorrect. The book says protein elevation starts 1-2 weeks after onset and peaks at 4-6 weeks.
Correct. The book describes GBS CSF as elevated protein (up to 500 mg/dL) with minimal or no increase in leukocytes, usually lymphocytes under 20/mcL.
questions.clue: CSF protein is high while the lymphocyte count is under 20/mcL.
questions.priority: Interpret CSF results in suspected GBS.

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barre syndrome is immobile in the ICU. For each intervention, indicate the complication it is mainly meant to prevent.
rows: Low-molecular-weight heparin
Repositioning every 2 hours
Chest physiotherapy
Skin care
rationales: Thromboembolism. The book lists low-molecular-weight heparin for DVT/PE prevention.
Pressure injury. The book says to reposition every 2 hours to prevent pressure injuries.
Respiratory complications. Chest physiotherapy is listed as pulmonary hygiene.
Pressure injury. Skin care is part of supportive care to protect immobile skin.
questions.clue: Each intervention targets a different complication of immobility.
questions.priority: Prevent the complications of immobility in GBS.

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barre syndrome is starting a plasmapheresis treatment. Which action by the nurse is most important during the treatment?
options: Leave the client alone to rest during the procedure
Encourage active exercise during the treatment
Monitor the client closely to detect complications
Hold all respiratory assessments until the treatment ends
rationales: Incorrect. The client needs close observation during treatment.
Incorrect. Active exercise is not appropriate for a client with flaccid weakness during a procedure.
Correct. The book calls for close monitoring during IVIG and plasmapheresis to detect complications.
Incorrect. Respiratory status needs continuous assessment in GBS.
questions.clue: The client is receiving plasmapheresis.
questions.priority: Monitor closely during GBS treatments to detect complications early.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which findings suggest cranial nerve involvement and a need for swallowing precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Facial droop
Tingling in the feet
Dysphagia
Trouble chewing
Sweating and flushing
Labile blood pressure
rationales: Correct. Facial droop is a cranial nerve finding the book says to watch for; facial weakness also makes it harder to control food in the mouth.
Incorrect. Tingling in the feet is a sensory symptom.
Correct. Dysphagia is a listed cranial nerve finding and directly raises aspiration risk.
Correct. Trouble chewing is a listed cranial nerve finding that makes safe eating harder.
Incorrect. Sweating and flushing are autonomic signs.
Incorrect. Labile blood pressure is an autonomic sign.
questions.clue: Some findings involve the face, chewing and swallowing; others are autonomic or sensory.
questions.priority: Recognize cranial nerve involvement that raises aspiration risk in GBS.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with Guillain-Barre syndrome who has flaccid paralysis of the legs. Which task is most appropriate to assign to the assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Measure the client's vital capacity
Assess for changes in the client's voice
Reposition the client every 2 hours
Monitor the client during plasmapheresis
rationales: Incorrect. Measuring and interpreting vital capacity is a respiratory assessment for the nurse or respiratory therapist.
Incorrect. Voice change is a respiratory red flag that the nurse must assess.
Correct. Repositioning every 2 hours is routine supportive care an AP can perform.
Incorrect. Close monitoring during treatment to detect complications requires nursing judgment.
questions.clue: Only one task is routine care without assessment.
questions.priority: Delegate routine repositioning; keep respiratory assessment and treatment monitoring with the nurse.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client who is using accessory muscles and cannot cough
A client with leg weakness who needs passive range-of-motion exercises
A client who reports tingling in both feet
A client whose Foley catheter bag needs to be emptied
rationales: Correct. Use of accessory muscles and inability to cough are red flags for respiratory collapse.
Incorrect. ROM exercises are routine care.
Incorrect. Paresthesia is an expected early symptom.
Incorrect. Emptying a drainage bag is routine.
questions.clue: One client shows red flags for respiratory collapse.
questions.priority: Respiratory compromise in GBS takes priority.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews medications for a client with Guillain-Barre syndrome. Which drug and purpose pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Antihypertensive: blood pressure control
Tricyclic antidepressant: neuropathic pain
Tricyclic antidepressant: reduce antibody levels
Antibiotic: treat infections
Low-molecular-weight heparin: DVT/PE prevention
rationales: Correct. Antihypertensives are listed for blood pressure control.
Correct. Tricyclic antidepressants are listed for neuropathic pain.
Incorrect. IVIG and plasmapheresis reduce antibody levels; tricyclics are for neuropathic pain.
Correct. Antibiotics are listed for infections.
Correct. LMWH is listed for DVT/PE prevention.
questions.clue: Each GBS medication has a specific purpose.
questions.priority: Match GBS medications to their purposes.

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barre syndrome has a distended bladder and has not voided for many hours. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
options: A Foley catheter to manage retention and monitor output
Restricting all oral fluids
Waiting until the client feels the urge to void
Giving a laxative
rationales: Correct. The book lists a Foley catheter to manage urinary retention and monitor output in the acute phase.
Incorrect. Restricting fluids does not relieve retention.
Incorrect. Urinary function may be impaired in GBS, so waiting is unsafe.
Incorrect. A laxative treats the bowel, not urinary retention.
questions.clue: The client has urinary retention.
questions.priority: Manage urinary retention in acute GBS.

questions.stem: A client recovering from Guillain-Barre syndrome says, "It's been weeks, and I'm still weak. I'm so frustrated. Will this ever end?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "You should be fully recovered by now."
"Try not to think about it, and you will feel better."
"There's nothing more that can be done for you."
"Recovery is often slow and can take months. It's understandable to feel frustrated."
rationales: Incorrect. This is inaccurate and adds to the client's frustration.
Incorrect. This dismisses the client's feelings.
Incorrect. This is inaccurate and removes hope.
Correct. The book says full recovery can take up to 200 days (p.149); giving an honest time frame and acknowledging frustration provides emotional support.
questions.clue: The client is frustrated by slow recovery.
questions.priority: Provide accurate information and emotional support for frustration in GBS.

questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barre syndrome has been treated for 1 week. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or worsening.
rows: Vital capacity has risen from 14 to 22 mL/kg
The client now has a strong, effective cough
The client is newly using accessory muscles to breathe
Weakness has spread from the arms to the trunk
Breathing is now even and unlabored instead of shallow and rapid
rationales: Improvement. A vital capacity below 15 mL/kg is a red flag; rising above it is improvement.
Improvement. Inability to cough is a red flag, so a strong cough is improvement.
Worsening. Use of accessory muscles is a red flag for respiratory collapse.
Worsening. Ascending weakness to the trunk shows progression.
Improvement. Shallow, rapid breathing is a red flag; even, unlabored breathing shows improvement.
questions.clue: Compare each finding with the book's respiratory red flags and ascending pattern.
questions.priority: Evaluate GBS response by respiratory status and progression of weakness.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with myasthenia gravis. Which findings increase the client's risk for aspiration? Select all that apply.
options: Trouble chewing
Difficulty swallowing
Diplopia
Ptosis
Jaw drop when fatigued
rationales: Correct. Bulbar weakness causes trouble chewing.
Correct. Difficulty swallowing is listed and raises aspiration risk.
Incorrect. Diplopia is an eye finding that does not affect swallowing.
Incorrect. Ptosis is an eye finding that does not affect swallowing.
Correct. Jaw drop when fatigued signals weakness of the chewing muscles.
questions.clue: Some findings involve bulbar muscles; others involve the eyes.
questions.priority: Recognize bulbar weakness that raises aspiration risk in MG.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the plan of care for a client with myasthenia gravis. For each item, indicate whether the nurse should carry it out as ordered or clarify it with the provider.
rows: Give pyridostigmine on time
Give prednisone as scheduled
Start a beta-blocker for blood pressure
Offer small, frequent meals after a rest period
rationales: Carry out. The book stresses giving anticholinesterase drugs such as pyridostigmine on time.
Carry out. Prednisone is listed among MG medications.
Clarify. The book lists beta-blockers among medications that can worsen MG symptoms.
Carry out. The book advises rest before meals and small, frequent meals.
questions.clue: One order involves a drug class the book says worsens MG.
questions.priority: Question medications that can worsen myasthenia gravis.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is eating lunch. Halfway through the meal, the client's jaw drops and the head bobs. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Encourage the client to eat faster before getting more tired
Stop the meal, let the client rest and assess for aspiration risk
Offer a large drink of water to help the food go down
Give the client a sedative to promote relaxation
rationales: Incorrect. Eating faster while fatigued raises aspiration risk.
Correct. Jaw drop and head bobbing are signs of fatigue, symptoms improve with rest, and the book prioritizes preventing aspiration.
Incorrect. A large drink with weak swallowing muscles raises aspiration risk.
Incorrect. The book says to avoid sedatives because they may worsen respiratory depression.
questions.clue: Jaw drop and head bobbing appear when the client is fatigued.
questions.priority: Prevent aspiration in MG by stopping activity and allowing rest.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis has sudden, severe generalized weakness. The nurse is preparing an SBAR report to the provider. Which information will best help the provider tell whether this is a myasthenic or a cholinergic crisis?
options: Whether the client has ptosis and double vision
Whether the client recently missed doses or took extra doses of pyridostigmine
The time of the client's last meal
The client's current pain rating
rationales: Incorrect. Ptosis and diplopia are common MG eye findings and do not tell the two crises apart.
Correct. The book says myasthenic crisis is due to undermedication and cholinergic crisis to overmedication.
Incorrect. Meal timing matters for aspiration risk but does not distinguish the crises.
Incorrect. Pain is not a feature that separates myasthenic from cholinergic crisis.
questions.clue: The two crises have opposite causes related to medication.
questions.priority: Include medication history in the SBAR report to help identify the type of crisis.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with myasthenia gravis. Which task can the nurse assign to the assistive personnel (AP)?
options: Teach the client about preventing cholinergic crisis
Help the client rest before meals and offer small, frequent meals
Assess the client's breath sounds
Evaluate the client's response to pyridostigmine
rationales: Incorrect. Teaching is a nursing responsibility.
Correct. Rest before meals and small, frequent meals are routine care measures an AP can support.
Incorrect. Respiratory assessment is a nursing responsibility.
Incorrect. Evaluating medication response requires nursing judgment.
questions.clue: Only one task is routine care without assessment, teaching or evaluation.
questions.priority: Delegate routine meal support; keep assessment, teaching and evaluation with the nurse.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for several clients with myasthenia gravis. For each finding, indicate whether it needs immediate action or can be followed up routinely.
rows: Severe weakness with dyspnea and cyanosis
Mild eyelid drooping that is worse in the evening
Diarrhea and bradycardia after the client took extra pyridostigmine
A request for help planning small, frequent meals
rationales: Immediate action. Severe weakness with dyspnea and cyanosis signals myasthenic crisis.
Routine follow-up. MG symptoms worsen during the day, so mild evening ptosis is expected.
Immediate action. Diarrhea and bradycardia after overmedication suggest cholinergic crisis.
Routine follow-up. Meal planning is important but not urgent.
questions.clue: Crisis findings differ from expected daily symptom changes.
questions.priority: Prioritize clients with signs of myasthenic or cholinergic crisis.

questions.stem: A client with well-controlled myasthenia gravis plans to get a vaccine next week and to have elective surgery next month. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
options: "Immunizations and surgery can both worsen MG symptoms, so plan them with your provider."
"Neither one will affect your myasthenia gravis."
"Stop taking pyridostigmine the week before each one."
"Only surgery can affect MG; vaccines never do."
rationales: Correct. The book lists immunizations and surgical procedures among factors that exacerbate MG.
Incorrect. The book lists both as exacerbating factors.
Incorrect. Stopping pyridostigmine risks undermedication and myasthenic crisis.
Incorrect. The book lists immunizations as an exacerbating factor.
questions.clue: The client plans two events that the book lists as exacerbating factors.
questions.priority: Teach clients with MG to plan around known exacerbating factors.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis says, "I've been so stressed about work, and my weakness is worse." Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Advise taking extra pyridostigmine on stressful days
Explore the client's stressors and ways of coping
Explain that emotional stress can worsen MG symptoms
Offer emotional support
Tell the client the weakness is probably imaginary
rationales: Incorrect. Extra doses can cause cholinergic crisis from overmedication.
Correct. Exploring stressors and coping supports the book's advice to avoid stress and provide emotional support.
Correct. The book lists emotional stress as an exacerbating factor.
Correct. The book includes emotional support in MG nursing care.
Incorrect. This dismisses a real effect of stress on MG.
questions.clue: The client links stress to worsening weakness.
questions.priority: Support coping and stress reduction in MG.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a client with generalized myasthenia gravis. Which treatments should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Prednisone
Plasmapheresis
Pyridostigmine
Carbidopa-levodopa
Thymectomy
Riluzole
rationales: Correct. Prednisone is listed among MG medications.
Correct. Plasmapheresis is listed to help stabilize symptoms.
Correct. Pyridostigmine is the anticholinesterase drug listed for MG.
Incorrect. Carbidopa-levodopa is used in Parkinson disease.
Correct. Thymectomy is listed to help stabilize symptoms and improve long-term survival.
Incorrect. Riluzole is used in ALS.
questions.clue: Only some of the listed treatments are used in MG.
questions.priority: Anticipate the medical and surgical treatments for MG.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis has lost weight because of chewing and swallowing problems. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage rest before meals
Serve one large meal after morning exercise
Monitor for signs of dehydration and malnutrition
Offer small, frequent meals
Schedule meals when the client is most tired
rationales: Correct. The book advises rest before meals.
Incorrect. MG weakness worsens with activity, so a large meal after exercise is harder to manage.
Correct. The book says to monitor for dehydration and malnutrition.
Correct. Small, frequent meals are recommended.
Incorrect. Symptoms are worse when fatigued, which raises aspiration risk.
questions.clue: The client is losing weight from chewing and swallowing weakness.
questions.priority: Support nutrition in MG with rest, small frequent meals and monitoring.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews factors the book associates with Bell palsy and trigeminal neuralgia. For each factor, indicate which condition it is associated with.
rows: Pregnancy
A recent viral infection
Older age
Attacks set off by wind or light touch
Emotional stress
rationales: Bell palsy. Pregnancy is listed as an associated factor for Bell palsy.
Bell palsy. The book says Bell palsy is likely viral and lists viral infection as a factor.
Trigeminal neuralgia. The book calls trigeminal neuralgia age-related.
Trigeminal neuralgia. Attacks are triggered by light touch or wind.
Bell palsy. Stress is listed as an associated factor for Bell palsy.
questions.clue: Each factor is linked to one of the two facial nerve disorders.

questions.stem: A client with new Bell palsy is upset about the appearance of one side of the face and says, "I look terrible. Will it stay like this?" Which responses by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: "This weakness means you had a stroke."
"Your face will stay paralyzed for the rest of your life."
"Bell palsy often begins to improve within about 3 weeks."
"Most people have a full or partial recovery."
"It is understandable to be upset about how your face looks."
rationales: Incorrect. Bell palsy affects the facial nerve (CN VII); it is not a stroke.
Incorrect. This contradicts the book's prognosis.
Correct. The book says Bell palsy improves within 3 weeks; most clients begin to recover in that time, though full recovery can take longer.
Correct. The book states the prognosis is usually full or partial recovery.
Correct. Acknowledging the client's feelings about appearance is supportive.
questions.clue: The client is distressed about facial appearance and the future.
questions.priority: Support body image with empathy and accurate prognosis.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an infant with a myelomeningocele. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected with the defect or should be reported as a possible complication.
rows: Paralysis of the legs
Bowel and bladder dysfunction
Head circumference that is increasing
Repeated vomiting
rationales: Expected. Paralysis is listed as a symptom of spina bifida.
Expected. Bowel and bladder dysfunction are listed spina bifida symptoms.
Report. An enlarging head is a sign of hydrocephalus, which spina bifida can lead to.
Report. Vomiting is a listed symptom of hydrocephalus and increased intracranial pressure.

questions.priority: Report signs of hydrocephalus in an infant with spina bifida.

concerns.issue: Chapter opener lists 'SPINAL BIFIDA & HYDROCEPHALUS' (should read 'Spina bifida'). The topic is covered only briefly on p.153 with no section number (after F12), while topics that do have sections (increased ICP F2, ALS F10) and the Bell palsy/trigeminal neuralgia table on p.153 are not listed in the opener.
Key Focus last bullet is missing its first word: 'management in neuromuscular disorders (MG, Guillain-Barre)' (likely 'Airway/respiratory management...').
Stroke Causes graphic lists 'High LDL' twice in the Risk Factors box.
Stroke Diagnosis graphic has two 'Echocardiography' tiles with the same content; the second contains the typo 'embolisn'.
Late signs list says 'decerberte' (should be 'decerebrate'); the 'ICP Memory Cheat: "ICP =' heading is left unfinished and the mnemonic letters (I, C, P, B, H) do not spell ICP.
Table 1 defines 'Focal nonmotor' as 'Other symptoms before movement'; nonmotor seizures are seizures without motor signs (e.g., sensory, autonomic, cognitive), so the description is inaccurate.
EEG is described as 'not helpful for acute status epilepticus'; EEG is commonly used in status epilepticus (e.g., to detect nonconvulsive seizures), so this statement is clinically questionable.
Monitoring box reads 'vomiting, lyres' - apparent typo (possibly 'fevers').
Meningitis Causes graphic lists Streptococcus pneumoniae as the newborn bacterial cause; in neonates group B Streptococcus is typically the leading cause, so this is clinically questionable.

CSF glucose ranges overlap: normal is given as 40-80 mg/dL (p.136) but the meningitis finding is 'low glucose (<45 mg/dL)', so 40-44 mg/dL would count as both normal and abnormal. Normal CSF protein is also 15-50 mg/dL here but 15-60 mg/dL on p.149 (GBS).
Assessment graphic heading is misspelled 'Encephalitits Assessment'.

Key Medications boxes are mislabeled: the 'Anticholinergic' box names no drug, while 'Atropine' appears in the 'Vasopressors' box; 'Inotropes (Dopamine, Norepinephrine)' sits inside the Methylprednisolone box. The methylprednisolone claim of improved motor/sensory recovery in SCI is also clinically debated.

'Alzheimer Disease (AD) Assessment.' is formatted as a bullet under Population Impact instead of a heading. Stage 1 is labeled 'Preclinical' but lists symptoms (memory loss, irritability, poor judgment), which is internally inconsistent.
Pharmacologic Highlights table: the 'Action' column actually holds drug classes/examples and the fourth column (the true action) has no header; 'manag ement' has a stray space.

The PD overview says treatments 'can slow progression' and p.143 lists 'prevent disease progression' as a goal, while p.143 also says treatment focuses on symptom management; current PD drugs are symptomatic, so the slowing claim is questionable.
'Urinaryretention' is missing a space; the 'MS SUCKS' mnemonic explains only the letters S-U-C-K-S.

ALS Causes graphic lists 'Viral Infection & Malnutrition' twice in Risk Factors. The box 'LOC: Most sensitive indicator of neurological status' appears in the ALS Remember box, where cognition and consciousness are described as unaffected.

GBS timing is inconsistent: Causes graphic says onset 1-3 weeks after infection while History says 2-4 weeks; Recovery says weakness may last 2-4 weeks while p.148 says paralysis usually lasts 4-8 weeks.
AChR antibodies are stated in the text as present in about 80% of MG patients, but the Diagnosis graphic on the same page says positive in 74%.

Heading reads 'Gravis Collaborative Care' (missing 'Myasthenia'). The text also says anticholinesterase drugs and prednisone manage symptoms 'by reducing autoimmune activity', but pyridostigmine does not reduce autoimmune activity.
The Bell palsy / trigeminal neuralgia comparison table has no heading or section number, and neither condition appears in the chapter opener.

The Meningitis Causes graphic says isolation precautions 'may be needed early in treatment', while p.137 says droplet precautions must be initiated immediately for bacterial meningitis; the two statements differ in strength.

The PD Causes graphic lists smoking (with caffeine) as a protective factor; presenting smoking as protective in a nursing review is questionable and could mislead health teaching. The claim that pesticides raise PD risk 'by up to 80%' is unsourced.
Selegiline is listed 'for neuroprotection'; a neuroprotective effect in PD is not established, so this is clinically questionable.

Plasmapheresis is listed with stem cell therapy as an 'experimental' MS treatment; plasmapheresis is an established rescue therapy for severe relapses, so grouping it as experimental is questionable (no question was built on the plasmapheresis claim).

'ALS = Locked-In Syndrome' conflates two different conditions; inappropriate laughing/crying is labeled 'bulbar palsy' though it describes pseudobulbar affect; and 'ALS is currently untreatable' conflicts with p.148, where riluzole prolongs survival.
Sensory loss is given as 'Pinprick test from T12 -> T6' with no explanation of what the range means.
'Pesticide exposure can mimic MG symptoms' is listed under Risk Factors, but something that mimics a disease is not a risk factor for it.
